title: Setting Aside Resources for Small Bets
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The argument starts from a structural observation about internal capital allocation: competing for resources is not a fair fight, because organisations over-invest in what is already working at the expense of what could be. Established groups and programmes attract the resources while new ideas face cautious, conservative investment, even though everyone acknowledges that an enterprise without new initiatives becomes vulnerable. The essay's remedy is procedural rather than exhortatory. Rather than asking leaders to be braver in the annual contest, it proposes parking money and talent in advance, specifically earmarked for untested ideas, on the explicit grounds that incumbents will rain on any parade they are not marching in and nascent initiatives almost always lose a straight fight. Replacing the single large gamble with many small bets is presented as what actually produces innovation. The second-order effect named at the end is the more interesting one: once people know the money exists, more ideas surface, which makes the reserve a demand-generating mechanism and not just a funding one.
points: The diagnosis is structural rather than a matter of courage: established programmes reliably beat new ideas in any open contest for resources, so the contest itself is the problem.
The remedy is to ring-fence money and talent in advance for untested ideas, removing them from a competition they are designed to lose.
Many small bets are preferred to the single large gamble, with the Hail Mary pass named as the pattern to replace.
The second-order effect is the sharper insight: visible earmarked resources cause more new ideas to surface, so the reserve generates demand rather than merely funding it.
The closing rule, that whatever leaders fund they get more of, makes budget allocation a statement of what the organisation will become.
quotes: Competing for resources is not a fair fight in most organizations — the rich always get richer.
Organizations tend to over-invest in what is working at the expense of what could be.
Talent and capital are hard to come by for champions of new ideas.
At any given time, they make several small bets and marshal the resources to allow those with an untested idea to explore the possibilities.
In any competition for resources, the nascent initiatives almost always lose.
When enterprises replace the Hail Mary pass by taking many small risks and bets, innovation blossoms.
Once everyone in the organization knows resources exist for a bright, new idea, more appear.
